name: Potato diet

card.summary: A short-term mono-diet of plain potatoes used to lose weight quickly, which looksmaxxers also try to slim the face and reduce water-related puffiness.
card.aka: potato hack, spud fit, potato mono-diet
card.note: Single-food diets can leave gaps in protein, fat and micronutrients; extended versions are discussed with medical supervision.

quick.overview:
The potato diet means eating mostly or only plain potatoes, usually boiled, baked or steamed without added fat, for a few days up to several weeks. People use it to drop weight fast, and because lower body fat is what makes jawlines, cheekbones and definition more visible, it is discussed as a route to a leaner face.

Proponents point to potatoes' low calorie density, fullness and potassium content. Looksmax.org posters have also tried it to reduce what they call facial bloat. Controlled trials have tested potato-rich low-energy-density diets, but not strict potato-only eating for appearance.
quick.how: The common version is short, three to five days, eating plain potatoes with water, tea or black coffee and little or no seasoning. Looser versions add small amounts of other whole plant foods, and some people extend the plan with medical oversight. After the diet, people usually return to a broader eating pattern.
quick.risks: Experts quoted in coverage note that a single-food diet can lack protein, healthy fats and micronutrients, and that long mono-diets risk malnutrition, constipation or diarrhoea, fatigue and muscle loss. Weight often returns after normal eating resumes, and clinicians warn that mono-diets can sometimes signal disordered eating.

lead: The potato diet is a mono-diet in which a person eats mainly or exclusively potatoes, typically plain and without added oils or toppings, for a limited time [1][2]. It is a way to lose weight quickly through low calorie intake and fullness, and for people interested in appearance, leaner body composition shows up in the face as a sharper jaw and cheek definition.

Modern interest grew through several public cases. In 2010 Chris Voigt of the Washington State Potato Commission ate around twenty potatoes a day for two months, and in 2016 magician Penn Jillette began a weight-loss programme with two weeks of potatoes before widening his diet [1]. Grokipedia adds that Australian Andrew Taylor ate only potatoes for a year in 2016 under medical supervision and reported a large weight loss, and that Tim Steele's 2016 book The Potato Hack promoted three to five day versions [2]. Community experiments later drew large discussions on Hacker News [5][6].

On looksmax.org, a poster starting a three-day potato diet said he hoped the potassium would reduce facial bloat and water retention and expected to lose about two pounds [4]. Clinical research has examined potato-containing low-energy-density diets in people with insulin resistance [3], but no controlled study has examined a potato-only diet for facial appearance.

chain: Less body and facial fat, sharper jaw and cheek definition
angle.text: People use it as a brief reset to cut calories quickly, and some also hope its potassium reduces water-related facial puffiness. Any change in the face follows from overall weight loss.

paras: The strictest forms permit only plain potatoes with water, plain tea or coffee and salt; looser forms add small amounts of other whole plant foods [2]. Proponents cite low calorie density, fibre, potassium, vitamin C and B6, and the satiety of boiled potatoes, and some mention resistant starch from cooled potatoes [2].
Wikipedia classes it as one example of a monotrophic diet, meaning a diet built around a single food [1].

Voigt's 2010 two-month experiment was meant to show potatoes are healthy; he accepted that the diet is not sustainable long term [1]. Jillette used a two-week potato phase in 2016 as a starting point for changing his habits rather than a permanent plan [1]. Grokipedia also links the idea to pre-famine Ireland, where potatoes supplied most calories, and to Mary McDougall's potato-centred plans [2].

A looksmax.org thread describes a three-day potato diet aimed at reducing facial bloat, with one reply wishing the poster luck and another dismissing bloat while joking about eating pizza, and a reply saying testimonials found online looked promising [4].

Wikipedia lists possible long-term risks of single-food diets as anaemia, osteoporosis, malnutrition and muscle catabolism, with constipation, diarrhoea, fatigue and worsened mood among side effects, and notes some experts say any mono-diet may signal a developing eating disorder [1]. Grokipedia says experts point to lack of balance across food groups and frequent weight regain [2].

No studies found of potato-only diets. A randomised 8-week feeding trial in adults with insulin resistance compared a low-energy-density diet high in potatoes with a bean-based equivalent and was titled as showing reductions in body weight and insulin resistance [3].

timeline.event: Chris Voigt eats about twenty potatoes a day for two months [1].
Penn Jillette starts a weight-loss plan with two weeks of potatoes; Andrew Taylor begins a year of potatoes; Tim Steele's The Potato Hack is published [1][2].
A potato diet community trial and its results are discussed on Hacker News [5][6].

lore.intro: Potato diet posts treat it as a short reset for weight and bloat [4].

claims.claim: A few days of potatoes reduces facial bloat through potassium
claims.believers: A poster expected the diet's potassium to clear facial bloat and water retention and lose around two pounds [4].
claims.experts: No published study has tested this; reviewers note single-food diets can cause nutrient gaps [1].

claims.claim: Potato-heavy eating produces rapid weight loss
claims.believers: Proponents point to satiety and low calorie density, and to cases such as Taylor and Jillette [2].
claims.experts: A controlled trial of low-energy-density potato-based diets found reductions in weight and insulin resistance [3]; Wikipedia notes no controlled studies of potato-only eating [1].
